← Actions Permissions Check

How to set least-privilege permissions for GitHub Actions

Set permissions: contents: read at the workflow level, then add the one extra scope a specific job needs directly on that job — for example pull-requests: write only on the job that comments on a PR — rather than granting every job the broader set.

Most workflows never mention permissions: at all:

name: ci
on: pull_request_target
jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: npm test

That job runs with whatever your repository's or organization's default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions are. Repositories created before 2023-02-02 default to read-write on every scope unless someone has since narrowed it in Settings → Actions → General. A workflow triggered by a pull request from a fork then runs with a token that can push commits or edit releases, even though this job only reads the checkout and runs tests.

1. Set a minimal default at the workflow level

Add a permissions: block near the top of the file, starting from contents: read — the narrowest grant most jobs actually need:

permissions:
  contents: read

Every job in the file now runs with exactly that, unless a specific job overrides it.

2. Escalate only on the job that needs more

If one job in the workflow needs to comment on a pull request, give that job the extra scope rather than widening the workflow-level default for every job:

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: npm test
  comment:
    permissions:
      contents: read
      pull-requests: write
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - run: gh pr comment ...

The build job still runs with the workflow-level contents: read; only comment gets the extra scope, and only for the duration of that job.

3. Avoid write-all

permissions: write-all grants every scope write access at once. It is explicit, which is better than nothing, but it is rarely what a job actually needs — replace it with the specific scopes the job's steps actually use.

4. Check every workflow at once

Paste your workflow YAML into Actions Permissions Check to find every workflow and job that still relies on the ambient default, or that grants write-all, across every file at once — or run the CLI in your own repository:

python3 check.py --fail-on-risk

That exits with a nonzero status if any workflow or job has no explicit permissions grant, or grants write-all — wire it into your own CI to block a newly-added unscoped workflow before it merges.

What this does not tell you

This tool cannot see your repository's or organization's actual default token setting — there is no public API for it — so an "unspecified" finding means the file doesn't say, not that your account is definitely misconfigured. And it never judges whether the scopes a workflow does declare are the minimum a job needs; deciding that is still yours to do.

No warranty. This page and the tool it describes are provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind. Verify before relying on the output. This is not a security audit or a compliance attestation, and it does not tell you your repository's actual default token permissions — only what a given workflow file does or does not make explicit.

Everything on the linked tool runs in your browser; nothing you paste is uploaded, and the tool makes no network calls of its own.

ACTIONS PERMISSIONS CHECK · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER

Does your GITHUB_TOKEN use least-privilege permissions?

A workflow or job with no permissions: block runs with whatever your repository or organization's default token permissions are — which can be read-write on every scope. Paste your workflow YAML below and this page finds every workflow and job that leaves that unspecified, or that grants permissions: write-all outright.

Nothing is uploaded. The YAML you paste is read in this browser and never leaves your device, and this tool makes no network calls of its own.

1. Paste one or more workflow files

Copy the contents of each file under .github/workflows/ you want checked. Add more blocks for more files — nothing here reads your repository, so pasting is how it sees anything.

Paste at least one workflow file above and click Check.

Findings

File : LineScopeStatusDetail / fix

Prefer a CLI, or want this in your own CI?

Same logic, zero dependencies, one file:

python3 check.py                  # scan .github/workflows under the current directory
python3 check.py /path/to/repo    # scan a specific checkout
python3 check.py --format json    # machine-readable
python3 check.py --fail-on-risk   # exit 2 if any write-all or unspecified grant is found

Get check.py from the repo — stdlib only, nothing to install, no network calls. Wire --fail-on-risk into your own CI to block a newly-added unspecified or write-all workflow before it merges.

Common questions

Why does a missing permissions: block matter?

A workflow or job with no permissions: key runs with whatever your repository or organization's default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions are set to. Many repositories still default to read-write on every scope — it was GitHub's own default for repositories created before 2023-02-02. A workflow triggered by something an outside contributor can influence then runs with a token that can push commits or modify repository settings, even if the job only needed to read the checkout.

What is permissions: write-all and why is it risky?

write-all explicitly grants every scope write access, which is broader than almost any job actually needs. It replaces an ambient, hidden default with an explicit, but still overly broad, grant.

Does this tool know my repository's actual default token permissions?

No. There is no public API for that setting, and this tool makes no network calls of any kind. An unspecified finding means the workflow file itself does not make the permissions explicit — it does not mean your repository is definitely misconfigured, only that this file does not say.

Does a clean scan mean my workflow is secure?

No. This checks one specific, well-documented thing: whether a permissions block exists and is not write-all. It does not judge whether the scopes a workflow does declare are the minimum a job actually needs, and it makes no claim about your repository's overall security or compliance posture.

What should I put in a permissions: block?

GitHub's own guidance is to start from contents: read at the workflow level and add only the specific scope a job needs, such as pull-requests: write for a job that comments on PRs. This tool does not decide that for you — it only tells you where nothing has been decided yet.

More: how to set least-privilege permissions for GitHub Actions. See also how this compares to OpenSSF Scorecard's Token-Permissions check and this checker vs. reading the workflow YAML by hand.

Want all ten workflow risks in one run? Workflow Audit is a single GitHub Action that checks them together.

It is not a security audit, a compliance attestation, or a guarantee that your CI is safe, and it does not replace a qualified professional. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

We do not promise uptime, backups of anything you type, or that a URL will keep working. Do not use this as a system of record. If a tool needs to survive, get check.py from the repo and run it yourself.

Everything runs in your browser. The YAML you paste is never uploaded; there are no accounts, cookies, or analytics vendors, and the tool makes no network calls. Anonymous feature events (check_run, example_loaded) are counted only in local storage and can be deleted with the button below. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

Least-privilege permissions are one piece of a hardened CI setup: Pinned Actions Check flags third-party uses: lines referenced by a mutable tag instead of a pinned commit SHA, Actions Injection Check flags pwn-request checkouts and script injection from untrusted ${{ github.event }} expressions, and Actions Secret Leak Check flags a step that transforms a secret before it can be masked, or exports one to $GITHUB_ENV/$GITHUB_OUTPUT without ::add-mask::. Actions timeout-minutes Check flags jobs with no timeout, which can hang and bill for six hours.

And if your workflows authenticate to AWS with OIDC rather than a stored access key, the permissions: block is only half the boundary — the other half is the IAM role's trust policy, which lives in your cloud account rather than this repository. OIDC Trust Policy Check reads that document and reports whether its sub condition actually pins the role to your repository and branch, or whether (for example) repo:owner/name:* has quietly admitted the pull_request context — and with it, a pull request opened from a fork.

A token's own scope is one axis of repository hardening; who a pull request actually gets routed to for review is a separate one. CODEOWNERS Shadow Checker resolves your CODEOWNERS file the way GitHub actually does — last matching pattern wins — and names every rule that never wins ownership of anything because a broader rule listed later always overrides it.

Keeping dependencies fresh is the other half: Dependabot Config Check lints your dependabot.yml and finds folders and ecosystems it never updates.

Free and open source. If this saved you from shipping an over-privileged token, the code is under an MIT licence — support is entirely optional and never changes what the tool does.

vs-openssf-scorecard.html.text:
← Actions Permissions Check

Actions Permissions Check vs. OpenSSF Scorecard

The same underlying question, two different shapes of answer. Scorecard's Token-Permissions check scores a whole repository's least-privilege posture using the GitHub API and a token, usually wired into CI. This page checks the same thing on one workflow file you paste, free, with no token, no install, and no network call of its own.

What each tool is for

OpenSSF Scorecard (github.com/ossf/scorecard) is an open-source project that runs 18 named checks against a repository -- among them Branch-Protection, Code-Review, Dangerous-Workflow, Vulnerabilities, Pinned-Dependencies, and Token-Permissions -- and scores each 0 to 10. The Token-Permissions check, per its own documentation, looks at whether a repository's workflows follow least privilege for the GITHUB_TOKEN, penalizing workflows that grant broader write access than a job appears to need, and returns one aggregate score for the repository. Running it needs a GitHub token to avoid API rate limits, and it is typically run through the ossf/scorecard-action in CI or read from Scorecard's own public dataset of already-scanned open-source repositories.

This checker does the narrower version of the same job: you paste the YAML of one or more workflow files, and it lists every workflow-level and job-level permissions: grant -- file, line, and whether it is explicit, write-all, or unspecified (running on the ambient repository/organization default). It runs entirely in your browser, needs no GitHub token and no install, and makes no network call of its own, so it works the same on a private repository's workflow, an unpushed fork, or a file from a repo you do not administer.

Where to answer each question.
QuestionWhere to answer it
How does my whole repository score across 18 supply-chain dimensions, tracked over time?OpenSSF Scorecard -- that is its entire job, and this tool does not attempt it.
Which exact workflow or job in one file has no permissions block, or grants write-all, and what should I put there instead?This checker -- a file:line table with an explicit/write-all/unspecified classification, not a score.
I need this to work on a private repository's workflow, or a file I have not pushed anywhere.This checker -- no token, no repository access, nothing leaves your browser. Scorecard's public dataset and default setup target public repositories.
I want one score I can track over time and compare against other repositories.OpenSSF Scorecard -- this tool produces a per-file finding list, not a trackable score.
I want this wired into CI to block a merge automatically.Either: Scorecard's own GitHub Action, or this tool's check.py --fail-on-risk for the permissions question specifically.

The two are complementary, not competing: a repository can run Scorecard for the ongoing 18-dimension score and still reach for this tool the moment the question is "which workflow or job, right now, and is it write-all or just unspecified" on a file that is not yet in a public, tokened CI run.

Run the free permissions check

Common questions

Should I use this checker or OpenSSF Scorecard?

They answer an overlapping question in different shapes. Scorecard is a broader, ongoing measurement: it runs 18 named checks against a repository -- Branch-Protection, Code-Review, Dangerous-Workflow, Token-Permissions, Vulnerabilities, Pinned-Dependencies, and more -- each scored 0 to 10, using the GitHub API and a token, usually wired into CI or read from Scorecard's own public dataset of already-scanned open-source repositories. This tool answers only the permissions question: you paste the YAML of a workflow file, and it lists every workflow or job with no explicit permissions block, or with permissions: write-all, file and line. It runs entirely in your browser, needs no token, no install, and no repository access, because it never talks to GitHub at all. If you want an ongoing score across 18 dimensions of a public repository's supply-chain posture, Scorecard is the right tool. If you want a fast, private, no-setup answer to the permissions question on one workflow file in front of you right now, this is the narrower tool for that.

Does Scorecard's Token-Permissions check do the same thing as this tool?

The underlying question is the same; the shape of the answer is not. Scorecard's own documentation describes Token-Permissions as checking whether a project's workflows follow the principle of least privilege for the GITHUB_TOKEN, and it returns one 0-to-10 score for the repository as a whole, penalizing write permissions that are broader than a job appears to need. This tool checks the same underlying fact -- an explicit permissions block versus an ambient default, and write-all specifically -- but instead of a score it lists every workflow-level and job-level grant individually, with the file, line, and its classification (explicit, write-all, or unspecified). Running both is not redundant: Scorecard's score reflects GitHub's live view of your repository and can move for reasons unrelated to the one file you are editing, while this tool's file:line list is exact for the YAML you actually pasted.

Why would I need a token-free, no-install checker if Scorecard already exists?

Three reasons this tool exists alongside it. First, Scorecard's CLI needs a GitHub token to avoid API rate limits in practice, and its GitHub Action needs to run inside your CI with repository access -- this tool needs neither, so it works on a workflow file from a private repository, a fork you have not pushed anywhere, or a repo you do not administer, with nothing leaving your browser. Second, Scorecard is a Go binary (or a container image) you install and configure; this tool is a page you open and paste into. Third, when the answer you actually want is "which workflow or job, and is it write-all or just unspecified," a single 0-to-10 repository score is a worse fit than a table naming every grant, which is the only thing this tool produces.

Is this page affiliated with OpenSSF or the Scorecard project?

No. This site is not affiliated with, endorsed by, or sponsored by the Open Source Security Foundation or the Scorecard project. Scorecard is an open-source project of the OpenSSF, named here only to describe what this checker is and is not, using facts drawn from Scorecard's own public documentation and source repository at github.com/ossf/scorecard.

No warranty. This tool is provided free and as-is, without warranty of any kind, express or implied. It is not a security audit, a compliance attestation, or a guarantee that your CI is safe, and it does not replace a qualified professional. You are responsible for reviewing and verifying its output before relying on it, including deciding what scopes a job actually needs. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for any loss or damage arising from its use.

Best-effort hosting, no SLA. These tools are free, experimental, and may be slow, broken, moved, or taken offline without notice. We do not promise uptime or that a URL will keep working.

Everything runs in your browser. The YAML you paste is never uploaded, and this page makes no live comparison against Scorecard -- it is a static page describing category facts sourced from Scorecard's own public documentation, not a live scan of any repository. We count only anonymous local feature events, never people or workflow content, with an opt-out on the checker page. Do Not Track and Global Privacy Control are honoured.

vs-reading-the-workflow-yaml-by-hand.htm.text:
← Actions Permissions Check

Actions Permissions Check vs. reading the workflow YAML by hand

This page names no company or product — reading a workflow file before trusting it is a habit most maintainers already have, not a competing tool. The gap is not carelessness: permissions inheritance in GitHub Actions is silent by design, and a manual read cannot show what a file does not contain.

What a manual read catches reliably

An obviously missing permissions: block at the top of a short, single-job workflow, or a permissions: write-all line sitting in plain view near the top of a file. Those are the cases a reviewer scanning top to bottom notices without much effort, and this tool does not replace that kind of reading.

What a manual read struggles with, and why

Where the two diverge on a real repository.
CaseReading by handThis checker
A job with no permissions: key of its ownSilently inherits the workflow-level block, or the repository default if there is none — a reader has to check two other places to know which, and nothing in the file states the repository default at allWalks the exact inheritance rule for every job and reports the source explicitly: its own grant, or "inherited from the workflow-level permissions"
A repository with dozens of workflow files, several jobs eachChecking every job in every file for an override is repetitive and exactly the kind of check attention degrades acrossScans every pasted file identically; job fifty gets the same treatment as job one
permissions: write-all on one job buried mid-fileEasy to miss once a reader has already judged the workflow-level block near the top to look fine and reads job bodies less closely afterwardFlags it by file and line regardless of where in the file it sits or what came before it
Distinguishing an explicit but narrow grant from an explicit but still-broad oneRequires holding "what scopes does this job actually need" in mind while reading unrelated YAML around itReports the exact scopes text for every explicit grant, so the narrowing judgment is made against a clean list, not while parsing indentation

None of this is about attention or diligence. Permissions inheritance is genuinely silent in the file format itself: a job's own missing key is not an error, it is a valid workflow that means something different depending on state the file does not contain.

Run the free permissions check

When to still read the file yourself

This tool only reports whether a permissions: key exists, whether it is write-all, and what scopes an explicit grant lists. It does not know your repository's or organization's actual default token permissions — there is no public API for that setting, and it makes no network call to check. It also does not decide whether the scopes a job does declare are the minimum that job needs; judging that against what each step in the job actually does is still a job for reading the workflow yourself.

Common questions

What does reading a workflow file by hand catch reliably?

An obviously missing permissions: block at the top of a short, single-job workflow, or a permissions: write-all line sitting in plain view. Those are the cases a reviewer scanning the file top to bottom is good at noticing, and this tool does not replace that kind of reading.

Why does job-level inheritance make a manual read unreliable across a real repository?

Because a job with no permissions: key of its own silently inherits the workflow-level block, or the repository's ambient default if the workflow has none either -- and nothing in the file tells a reader which case applies without checking two other places first: whether the workflow itself declares permissions:, and, if not, what the repository or organization default is set to (which no workflow file states at all). A reviewer has to hold that inheritance chain in their head correctly for every job in every file; a scanner walks the same chain the same way every time and never loses count partway through a fifty-job file.

Does file count matter, or is this only about complex single files?

Both. A repository with dozens of workflow files each defining several jobs turns a permissions review into checking every job in every file for an override, which is exactly the kind of exhaustive, repetitive check a reviewer's attention is worst at sustaining across many similar-looking blocks. A tool that scans every pasted file the same way does not get less careful on file thirty than it was on file one.

Is write-all always easy to spot by eye?

It is easy to spot when it sits at the top of a short file. It is easy to miss when it appears on one job buried in the middle of a long file with several other jobs around it, especially if a reader has already concluded from the workflow-level block near the top that the file looks fine and stops reading job bodies closely after that.

Does a clean scan from this tool mean my repository's default token permissions are safe?

No. This tool has no API access and does not know your repository's or organization's actual default GITHUB_TOKEN permissions -- there is no public API for that setting. An unspecified finding means the pasted file itself does not make permissions explicit; it does not mean the ambient default it would fall back to is necessarily broad, and a clean, all-explicit result says nothing about whether the scopes that are declared are the minimum each job actually needs.
